strengths_deep_dive: The primary strength of IIIT lies in its high program expense ratio, which reached <cite id="12">96.6% in FY2023</cite>. This indicates that nearly all funds are utilized for academic research and educational initiatives rather than administrative overhead. The organization has maintained a <cite id="11">100% independent board</cite>, ensuring a high level of governance oversight for its scholarly activities. Its academic contributions are substantial, with recent publications including <cite id="1">Islamic Legal Methodology: A New Perspective on Usul al-Fiqh</cite> and various works on the <cite id="4">Islamic vision of development</cite>. These works are distributed internationally, including through the <cite id="5">Bangladesh Institute of Islamic Thought</cite>.
rich_narrative.summary: The International Institute of Islamic Thought (IIIT) operates as a specialized academic center focused on the intellectual development of Islamic thought and education. While the organization maintains a <cite id="12">program expense ratio of 95.0%</cite>, its overall profile is constrained by significant reporting delays and limited transparency. No financial filings newer than FY2023 are available — donors should treat this <cite id="12">3-year-old financial picture</cite> with caution. The organization's primary output is scholarly research, having produced <cite id="3">over 600 scholarly titles</cite> to date. However, the financial health of the institution is currently under pressure. In the most recent reported period, <cite id="12">revenue declined by 45%</cite>, falling from over $16 million to <cite id="12">$8,955,918 in FY2023</cite>. This sharp decrease in funding coincides with a period where <cite id="12">total liabilities of $575,178</cite> slightly exceed <cite id="12">total assets of $551,681</cite>, indicating a precarious balance sheet. Furthermore, while IIIT claims an international mission, <cite id="12">95.0% of expenses remain within the United States</cite>, which may not align with donors seeking direct international impact. The organization's work is primarily academic, including the <cite id="1">Advancing Education in Muslim Societies (AEMS)</cite> initiative and various student training programs, but it lacks a <cite id="11">documented theory of change</cite> to connect these research activities to measurable social outcomes.
